hvtiRpropensity: Propensity Score Methods for Cardiac Surgery Studies

Source: R/help.R
hvtiRpropensity-package.Rd

Provides functions for propensity score and balancing score analysis used in cardiac surgery comparative-effectiveness research. Translates the Cleveland Clinic HVTI SAS template library into a consistent R workflow.

Step 1: estimate scores:

  • ps_logistic(): binary treatment propensity score (logistic regression; supports multiply-imputed data via a stacked data frame).

  • ps_forest(): binary treatment propensity score from a random forest (randomForestSRC), scored out-of-bag.

  • ps_ordinal(): ordered treatment propensity score (proportional-odds model via MASS::polr; equivalent to SAS PROC LOGISTIC default for ordinal responses).

  • ps_nominal(): nominal treatment propensity score (multinomial logistic via nnet::multinom; equivalent to SAS PROC LOGISTIC link=glogit).

  • bs_continuous(): balancing score for a continuous exposure (linear regression; equivalent to SAS PROC REG + %grp macro).

  • bs_count(): balancing score for a count exposure (negative-binomial or Poisson regression; equivalent to SAS PROC GENMOD dist=nb).

Outcome models:

  • fit_logistic(): binary, ordinal or nominal outcome-model bundle, with Rubin pooling over stacked imputations and Barnard-Rubin degrees of freedom, matching mice::pool().

  • fit_linear(): linear outcome-model bundle, with Rubin pooling.

  • validate_logistic(): applies a saved binary bundle to a validation cohort without refitting.

Step 2: balance and use scores:

  • ps_match(): 1:1 nearest-neighbour matching on a pre-computed score, on the probability or the logit scale. scale = "logit", caliper_sd = 0.2 is the Austin (2011) caliper. Returns a pair_id column in $data for use with sa_rosenbaum() and ps_rmst().

  • ps_weight(): IPTW weights (ATE / ATT / ATC) from a pre-computed score.

  • ps_support(): compares common-support and trimming rules.

  • ps_rmst(): restricted mean survival contrast, weighted, or on the matched pairs of a ps_match() object.

Balance statistics:

  • ps_stddiff(): standardized differences by variable type, optionally weighted (CCF %stddiff).

  • ps_stddiff_perm(): permutation reference for those differences (CCF %stddiffci).

  • ps_mw_var(): matching-weight difference in means with a bootstrap SD (CCF %mw_var).

Step 3: sensitivity analysis (optional):

  • sa_rosenbaum(): Rosenbaum gamma bounds for matched analyses; how much hidden bias would overturn the result.

  • sa_evalue(): E-values (VanderWeele & Ding 2017) for unmeasured confounding. Odds and hazard ratios need rare.

  • sa_overlap(): overlap and positivity diagnostics on the score distribution.

  • sa_trim_sweep(): how the effective sample size and the weights change across IPTW trim thresholds.

Data: sample_ps_data(), sample_ps_data_ordinal(), sample_ps_data_nominal() and sample_ps_data_count() generate synthetic datasets; is_ps_data() tests for a ps_data object.

Every function except the four data generators (which return data frames) and is_ps_data() returns a ps_data S3 object. Its $data slot holds the input data with any score, weight or flag columns appended, $meta records the columns and parameters used, and $tables holds the diagnostics: SMD tables, group counts, effective sample sizes, or a sensitivity function's bounds and sweeps.

hvtiPlotR::hv_mirror_hist() reads the $data of a ps_match() or ps_weight() object directly. hvtiPlotR::hv_balance() does not read $tables as they are: it needs one long data frame with variable, group and std_diff columns, the difference in percent, so the SMD tables are stacked and multiplied by 100 first. The vignette shows the reshape.

The SAS programs this package ports ship with it, in system.file("sas-templates", package = "hvtiRpropensity").

Typical two-step workflow (binary treatment)

library(hvtiRpropensity)

# Step 1: estimate propensity score
dta   <- sample_ps_data(n = 500, seed = 42)
dta$prob_t <- NULL
score <- ps_logistic(
  tavr ~ age + female + ef + diabetes + hypertension,
  data = dta
)
print(score)

# Step 2a: match on the logit of the score, caliper 0.2 SD
m <- ps_match(score$data, score_col = "logit_t", scale = "logit",
              caliper_sd = 0.2, seed = 42)
matched <- m$data[m$data$match == 1L, ]

# Step 2b: or weight
w <- ps_weight(score$data, score_col = score$meta$score_col)

References

Austin PC (2011). Optimal caliper widths for propensity-score matching when estimating differences in means and differences in proportions in observational studies. Pharmaceutical Statistics, 10(2), 150–161. doi:10.1002/pst.433

See also

  • ps_logistic(), ps_forest(), ps_ordinal(), ps_nominal(): propensity score estimation

  • bs_continuous(), bs_count(): balancing scores for continuous and count exposures

  • fit_logistic(), fit_linear(), validate_logistic(): outcome models

  • ps_match(), ps_weight(): matching and IPTW weighting

  • ps_stddiff(), ps_stddiff_perm(), ps_mw_var(): balance statistics

  • ps_support(), ps_rmst(): support rules and survival contrasts

  • sa_rosenbaum(), sa_evalue(), sa_overlap(), sa_trim_sweep(): sensitivity analysis

  • sample_ps_data(): synthetic dataset for examples / tests

  • is_ps_data(): predicate for ps_data objects
